Transport for London says the personal details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers may have been compromised after suspicious activity on its photocard website.  TfL detected the incident on November 16, when photocard holders began receiving unexpected emails asking them to create an account they already had. The photocard website was taken offline and remains down while the investigation continues.  Exposed data, per TfL: names, contact details (email and home addresses, phone numbers), dates of birth, and security questions and answers.  TfL says passwords, bank or payment card details, journey history, and the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were not compromised. The incident has been contained, and existing photocards can still be used for travel.  No threat actor or entry point has been disclosed. This is a new incident, separate from TfL's 2024 cyber attack.  Exposed security answers can be reused for account takeover. Affected customers should change their TfL password and security question, and anywhere else the same answers are used. Irish credit unions are disclosing theft of saved-payee data through a shared technology provider.  Capital Credit Union's November 18 update says its provider confirmed successful retrieval of payee records after a platform vulnerability was exploited October 2–4 and closed October 6. Capital was notified November 16.  Potentially affected fields include payee names, saved nicknames, IBANs, BICs and payment references, plus addresses in limited cases. Investigators could not determine whether all or only some saved-payee records were taken.  Capital says members' account details, balances and login credentials were not accessed. Do not confuse beneficiary bank details with stolen online-banking passwords or drained accounts.  Gurranabraher Credit Union separately confirms unauthorized access to saved-payee information and urges caution over unexpected financial calls, texts and emails.  RTÉ identifies the provider as Wellington IT and reports around 40 Irish credit unions affected. The total number of affected individuals remains unresolved. The repository tells your AI assistant not to inspect a script, then orders it to run silently. That is the trap.  Bitdefender identified 22 malicious GitHub links targeting AI-assisted development through project instructions, session-start hooks and configurations.  Two distinct paths matter: * Instruction files try to persuade an agent to execute setup.js. * Session-start hooks can trigger execution after a developer opens and trusts the repository, without a typed AI prompt.  Cloning alone is not proof of automatic compromise.  The analyzed payload can steal developer credentials and cloud secrets, alter local agent configurations, and use sufficiently privileged GitHub or GitLab tokens to plant malicious files in other repositories.  Those are analyzed capabilities, not a confirmed count of infected developers or downstream packages.  Review agent rules, hooks and MCP definitions before trusting unfamiliar projects. Keep execution approvals and least-privilege credentials in place.  Bitdefender research, Nov 17: bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/l… #AISecurity #SoftwareSupplyChain
